pos: n. (a Levite of the sons of Asaph who was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer after the captivity; also the original name of king Zedekiah, and of several other men)
etymology: From Hebrew Mattanyah, gift of the LORD, from mattan, a gift, and the divine name Yah. It was the birth-name of Judah's last king: Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah king and changed his name to Zedekiah (2Ki 24:17), a heathen monarch renaming a son of David as an act of ownership.
biblical_def: Mattaniah is a name worn by singers, gatekeepers, penitents and one doomed king, and its most memorable bearer holds a post described in a single clause of great beauty: “And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer” (Neh 11:17). Somebody has to start. In a congregation newly returned from seventy years in Babylon, standing in a city with broken walls before a house that made the old men weep, one Levite of Asaph's line was appointed to lead off the praise. He is named again in the roll of the Levites who came up with Zerubbabel: “Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, which was over the thanksgiving, he and his brethren” (Neh 12:8). The Chronicler traces the same family back into David's choir, where the ninth of the twenty-four courses fell to a Mattaniah of the sons of Heman (1Ch 25:16), and another Mattaniah of the sons of Asaph helped cleanse the house under Hezekiah (2Ch 29:13). A less happy Mattaniah appears in Ezra's list of those who had taken strange wives and put them away (Ezr 10:26). The thread through all of them is service in the house of God across five centuries, by men whose name means gift of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Mattaniah; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites and singers, and the original name of Zedekiah king of Judah.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that thanksgiving in the assembly is an appointed office and a duty, not a mood that must be waited for.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mattaniah is a Levite in a register and nobody has contested him. What his post sets against the modern congregation is the idea that praise is an ordered work. Nehemiah does not record that the people felt thankful; he records that a man was appointed to begin the thanksgiving in prayer, that he had brethren under him, that they were maintained by daily portions, and that the whole arrangement went back to the commandment of David the man of God. Thanksgiving in Scripture is a discipline with a rota attached.

The principle to recover is that duty leads and feeling follows. The psalms command it upon the soul rather than waiting on it: “Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name” (Psa 103:1). Hebrews makes it a sacrifice offered continually: “By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name” (Heb 13:15). A church that will only sing when it is moved has confused worship with sentiment; the returned exiles, who had every reason for grief and sang anyway, understood the thing better. Somebody had to begin, and it was Mattaniah's job.

pos: n. (a chief of the Levites in the return under Ezra, entrusted with the holy vessels; a name borne also by rulers, officers and singers of the tribe of Levi)
etymology: From Hebrew Chashabyah, the LORD hath considered or whom the LORD regardeth, from chashab, to think, reckon, esteem, with Yah. The same verb is the one Genesis uses when the LORD counted Abraham's faith to him for righteousness.
biblical_def: Hashabiah is one of the working names of the tribe of Levi, and the men who bore it turn up wherever something had to be carried, governed or sung. In Ezra's caravan he is one of the Merarite chiefs recruited at the river Ahava: “And Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty” (Ezr 8:19), and then one of the twelve to whom the treasure was committed for a journey of four months without an escort: “Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them” (Ezr 8:24). In Nehemiah he is a civil ruler taking his turn on the wall: “Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part” (Neh 3:17). He is among the chief of the Levites appointed “to praise and to give thanks, according to the commandment of David the man of God, ward over against ward” (Neh 12:24). An earlier Hashabiah of the Hebronites commanded seventeen hundred officers west of Jordan “in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king” (1Ch 26:30) — a phrase which is itself a small doctrine of vocation, the sacred and the civil work of one man named in one breath.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hashabiah; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites, one of whom carried the treasure up from Babylon with Ezra.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the business of the LORD and the service of the king are two lawful callings that God has given to the same men, and that the church impoverishes itself by grading one above the other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hashabiah is a Levite of the lists and nobody has contested him. What the Chronicler's phrase sets against a persistent churchly instinct is the flat pairing of “the business of the LORD” with “the service of the king” as the joint description of one man's office. The same Levites who sang the psalms judged causes, kept treasuries, commanded officers and rebuilt a wall. Nehemiah's roll of the builders is a roll of goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants, rulers of districts and priests, each repairing over against his own house.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of vocation as the Reformers recovered it. The medieval church divided life into the religious and the secular and reserved holiness for the cloister; Luther and Calvin answered that the milkmaid and the magistrate serve God in their callings as truly as the preacher in his. Paul states it as a rule for everyone: “whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31), and “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). Hashabiah carried silver four months across a dangerous road because it was the business of the LORD, and he counted the mile-markers as carefully as he sang the psalm.

pos: n. (the head of a family of three hundred seventy and two who returned from the captivity; also a son of David, and one of the princes who cast Jeremiah into the dungeon)
etymology: From Hebrew Shephatyah, the LORD hath judged, from shaphat, to judge or vindicate, with Yah. The verb is the one behind shophet, a judge, and behind the title of the book of Judges.
biblical_def: Shephatiah heads one of the families counted twice in the register of the return, with the same figure both times: “The children of Shephatiah, three hundred seventy and two” (Ezr 2:4), and again “The children of Shephatiah, three hundred seventy and two” (Neh 7:9). A second contingent of the house came up later with Ezra: “And of the sons of Shephatiah; Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him fourscore males” (Ezr 8:8). The name is borne by better and worse men. One Shephatiah was the fifth son born to David in Hebron (2Sa 3:4). Another was a son of Jehoshaphat, killed with his brothers by Jehoram (2Ch 21:2-4). And one is among the four princes who heard Jeremiah preaching surrender and demanded his death: “Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people” (Jer 38:1), and it was on their motion that the prophet was let down into the miry dungeon of Malchiah. The name means the LORD hath judged, and one man who bore it was in the room when a nation refused the word of the LORD's judgment and threw the messenger into a pit.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the register of the returned is a real census of real households, and that God preserves His church by families and by name.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Shephatiah is a family head in a census and nobody has contested him. What the register sets against a modern reader who skims it is the character of God's preservation of His people. The list is not round. Three hundred seventy and two, ninety and eight, two thousand fifty and six, an hundred thirty and nine — awkward numbers, counted twice, seventy years apart, and agreeing. Somebody kept those books through the captivity, and the Holy Ghost saw fit to put them in the canon.

The principle to recover is that the church is not an abstraction but a named people. The Lord “calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out” (Joh 10:3); the book of life has names written in it; Paul ends his epistles with rolls of greetings that no editor would have invented. A congregation that keeps no membership roll, knows no households, and cannot say who belongs to it has drifted from the pattern of a book that troubled to record that the children of Shephatiah were three hundred seventy and two.

pos: n. (the head of the largest lay family in the register of the return, two thousand an hundred seventy and two of whose children came up from Babylon; written Pharosh in Ezra 8)
etymology: From Hebrew Par'osh, a flea — the same word David uses when he asks Saul, after whom is the king come out? after a flea? A house of more than two thousand souls bore the name of the least considerable insect in the Hebrew language.
biblical_def: Parosh heads the first and largest family in the great register of those who came up with Zerubbabel: “The children of Parosh, two thousand an hundred seventy and two” (Ezr 2:3), and Nehemiah's copy of the roll gives the identical figure (Neh 7:8). A further company came later with Ezra: “Of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh; Zechariah: and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty” (Ezr 8:3). The house appears at every stage of the restoration. Seven of its men are named among those who had taken strange wives and put them away (Ezr 10:25), which is the register recording the sin of its largest family rather than hiding it. One of them worked on the wall: “After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh” (Neh 3:25). And the head of the house stands first among the chief of the people who set their seal to the covenant Nehemiah drew up: “The chief of the people; Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Zatthu, Bani” (Neh 10:14). Two thousand people named after a flea went home to a ruined city, repaired a wall, confessed a national sin, and signed a covenant.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the restoration was carried out by ordinary households of no distinction, and that the covenant is sealed by such people rather than by the eminent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Parosh is a family head in a census and nobody has contested him. What his house sets against the modern instinct is the ordinariness of the people God uses. The whole return was carried out by families with names like flea, whose only recorded qualifications were that they went, that they built, that they confessed and that they signed. There is no hero in Ezra 2. There is a list, and the list is the point.

The principle to recover is Paul's: “For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called” (1Co 1:26), because God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty. The temple that these families rebuilt was so plain that the men who remembered the first one wept aloud when they saw the foundation (Ezr 3:12), and Haggai had to ask them, is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing? Into that second and poorer house the Lord of glory Himself would one day walk. God builds with fleas.

pos: n. (the head of a family of six hundred twenty and three who returned with Zerubbabel, whose house appears again with Ezra and at the sealing of the covenant)
etymology: From Hebrew Bebay, of uncertain derivation, most likely a Babylonian or Persian name taken up during the exile — as several of the family names in the register appear to be. That is itself a small witness to where these households had been living.
biblical_def: Bebai is one of the middling houses of the return, and the register is exact about it: “The children of Bebai, six hundred twenty and three” (Ezr 2:11). Nehemiah's copy gives six hundred twenty and eight, one of the small divergences between the two rolls that a forger harmonising his documents would have removed and a faithful copyist of two separate registers would not. A second company came up with Ezra: “And of the sons of Bebai; Zechariah the son of Bebai, and with him twenty and eight males” (Ezr 8:11). Four men of the house are listed among those who had married strange wives (Ezr 10:28), and the head of the family sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:15). That is the whole record: a name, two counts, a small second migration, a sin confessed, and a signature. It is the ordinary shape of a Christian household in any century — numbered, mixed, repentant, and bound by covenant to the God of its fathers.

corruption_summary: The small numerical differences between the registers in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are offered as proof that Scripture contains errors. They are what two genuine documents of two different dates look like, and inerrancy has never meant that a copyist's numeral cannot slip.
corruption_paragraphs: The two rolls of the returned agree in most figures and differ in perhaps eighteen, and the difference is regularly produced as a straightforward contradiction. Two answers are worth stating plainly, and neither is special pleading. First, the lists are not the same document: Ezra 2 registers those who set out or were enrolled at one point, Nehemiah 7 reproduces a register he found (Neh 7:5) at a later date, after decades in which families had died out, arrived late, or been reckoned differently — and the totals in both are stated as the same grand figure, which shows the compilers were aware of their own arithmetic. Second, the doctrine of inerrancy has always been confessed of the original autographs, and the transmission of Hebrew numerals is precisely the class of detail most liable to a scribe's slip.

What must not be conceded is the inference the objection is built to carry — that because a numeral may vary, the Bible is a merely human book to be sifted for what a reader finds credible. The Scriptures are God-breathed, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16), and the Lord Himself rested an argument on a single word of a psalm and said “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). Six hundred twenty and three, or eight: either way, God knew which of Bebai's children went home.

pos: n. (one of the leaders who came up with Zerubbabel, and the head of a family of two thousand fifty and six in the register of the return)
etymology: From Hebrew Bigvay, evidently a Persian name; forms close to it appear in the Persian records of the period as the name of a provincial governor. Its presence at the head of an Israelite house is a mark of the generations spent under a foreign crown.
biblical_def: Bigvai appears twice over in the record of the return, once as a man and once as a house. He is named in the short list of those who led the first caravan home: “Which came with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, Baanah” (Ezr 2:2) — eleven leaders, and one of them called Nehemiah and another Mordecai, though neither is the man of the later books. His family is the second largest on the roll: “The children of Bigvai, two thousand fifty and six” (Ezr 2:14). A last remnant of the house came up with Ezra some eighty years afterward: “Of the sons also of Bigvai; Uthai, and Zabbud, and with them seventy males” (Ezr 8:14) — two named men and seventy others, from a house that had sent two thousand. Most of them had stayed in Babylon, and Scripture records the number without comment. Bigvai the chief signed the covenant at the end: “Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin” (Neh 10:16).

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that most of the exiles never came home, that Scripture records this plainly, and that a comfortable captivity is harder to leave than a cruel one.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bigvai is a name in the register and nobody has contested him. What the arithmetic of his house sets against the reader is a sobering fact the books of Ezra and Nehemiah never soften. Two thousand fifty and six of the children of Bigvai went up in the first company; when Ezra gathered a second caravan generations later, the house could raise seventy males. The rest of the Jews in Babylon — a great many more than ever returned — stayed. They had houses, trades, gardens and a settled life in the land Jeremiah had told them to build in, and when the decree of Cyrus opened the road, they did not take it.

The principle to recover is that prosperity holds men more firmly than persecution. Israel in Egypt cried out under the taskmasters; Israel in Babylon was comfortable and would not move. The Lord names the same danger for the church: the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word (Mar 4:19), and He said plainly, “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:62). The seventy who came up with Uthai and Zabbud left a great deal behind to do it, and the register writes their number down.

pos: n. (the head of a family of two hundred twenty and three in the register of the return, and one of the men who stood at Ezra's left hand when the law was read to the people)
etymology: From Hebrew Chashum, from a root meaning to be rich or opulent — hence wealthy. The name is worn by a returning household and by one of the fourteen men who stood on the wooden pulpit with Ezra at the reading of the law.
biblical_def: Hashum is one of the lesser houses of the return — “The children of Hashum, two hundred twenty and three” (Ezr 2:19) — and seven of its men are named among those who put away strange wives: “Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei” (Ezr 10:33). But the verse the name is worth remembering for is the one that describes the greatest day of public worship in the whole restoration. On the first day of the seventh month, in the street before the water gate, the people asked Ezra to bring the book, and the text records the platform and everyone who stood on it: “And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam” (Neh 8:4). Hashum stood on the left. The reading lasted from morning until midday, the Levites gave the sense so that the people understood, and the congregation wept and then feasted because the joy of the LORD was their strength. The head of the house afterward sealed the covenant (Neh 10:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hashum; in sacred history he is the head of a returning family, and one who stood by Ezra at the reading of the law.
webster_full: HASHUM, n. Wealthy, opulent; the head of a family of the children of Israel.
Two hundred twenty and three of his children returned from the captivity.
Seven of the sons of Hashum had taken strange wives, and put them away.
A Hashum stood upon the pulpit of wood at Ezra's left hand when the law was read.
The name is among those that sealed the covenant with Nehemiah.
scriptures: The children of Hashum, two hundred twenty and three.
Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.

And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah 8 is often cited as a warrant for whatever a congregation wishes to do in worship. What it actually establishes is the reading and exposition of Scripture as the centre of public worship, done from a pulpit, by qualified men, until the people understand.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is quoted in support of everything from open-air festivals to spontaneous liturgy, usually on the strength of its emotion. Read it for what it institutes. A platform is built for the purpose; a qualified man stands on it with named assistants; the book is opened and all the people stand up; the reading runs from morning until midday; the Levites cause the people to understand, reading distinctly and giving the sense; the people answer Amen, Amen and bow their heads and worship (Neh 8:6). That is the regulative principle at work — word, exposition, response — and the pulpit of wood is in the text.

The principle to recover is the primacy of preaching as the ordinary means God uses. Paul charges Timothy, “Give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13), and, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2). The day at the water gate produced tears first and then feasting, and both came out of the same cause: people finally understood what the book said. A service arranged so that the sermon must be short and the book need not be understood has inverted the order Nehemiah 8 lays down, whatever the emotion it produces.

pos: n. (the head of a family called Ater of Hezekiah, ninety and eight of whom returned from the captivity; also the head of a house of the porters)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ater, from 'atar, to shut up or bind — hence shut up, lame, or left-handed, since the related idiom describes a man bound in his right hand. Two distinct houses bear the name in the register: Ater of Hezekiah among the people, and Ater among the porters.
biblical_def: Ater is remembered by a phrase that has puzzled readers for centuries: “The children of Ater of Hezekiah, ninety and eight” (Ezr 2:16), repeated exactly in Nehemiah's roll (Neh 7:21). Whether Hezekiah was a further ancestor, or the family claimed descent from the good king of Judah, the register does not explain — and its unwillingness to explain is characteristic. Ezra copies what the record said. A second Ater heads a house of gatekeepers: “The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub” (Ezr 2:42), a hundred and thirty-nine doorkeepers in all. And Ater sealed the covenant with the chief of the people: “Ater, Hizkijah, Azzur” (Neh 10:17), where Hizkijah is the Hebrew of the same name as Hezekiah, standing next to him in the list. Ninety-eight people is a very small house. They are written down anyway, twice, with a note attached that nobody can now fully explain, because they were there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ater; in sacred history he is the head of a family called Ater of Hezekiah, and of a house of the porters, in the register of the return.
webster_full: ATER, n. Shut up, bound; the head of a family of the children of Israel.
The children of Ater of Hezekiah were ninety and eight in the register of the return.
The same number is given in the parallel roll in Nehemiah.
A house of the porters is also called the children of Ater.
Ater is named among those that sealed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah.
scriptures: The children of Ater of Hezekiah, ninety and eight.
The children of Ater of Hezekiah, ninety and eight.

The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that a faithful record keeps what it does not understand, and that a Bible edited down to what its editors could explain would be a smaller and a poorer book.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ater is a family head in a census and nobody has contested him. What the phrase Ater of Hezekiah sets before the reader is the honesty of the register. A compiler tidying his sources would have dropped or explained an obscure qualifier; Ezra transcribes it and moves on, and Nehemiah's independent copy has it too. The same is true across Scripture: unexplained names, unresolved details, hard sayings left standing. The text bears every mark of having been received rather than composed.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency and the honesty of Scripture together. “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deu 29:29). There is a great deal in the Bible a careful reader cannot fully account for — and the response of faith is neither to pretend the difficulty away nor to cut the passage out, but to do the words that are plain. Ninety-eight souls from a house whose second name nobody can now explain went home to Jerusalem, and God had their number written down.

pos: n. (a Levite who stood upon the stairs and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD in the great confession of Nehemiah 9; also a priest who blew with the trumpets before the ark)
etymology: From Hebrew Shebanyah, understood as the LORD hath grown him up or increased by the LORD, from a root meaning to grow, with Yah. Several men of the name serve in the restoration, all of them Levites or priests.
biblical_def: Shebaniah belongs to the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, the day of the great confession, when the children of Israel assembled with fasting and with sackcloth and earth upon them, separated themselves from strangers, and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers for a fourth part of the day, and read in the book of the law for another fourth part. Two lists of Levites are given, and he is in both: “Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” (Neh 9:4), and then in the summons to praise: “Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise” (Neh 9:5). What follows is the longest prayer in the Old Testament, a recital of the whole history of God's dealing with Israel from Abram to that morning, ending in a sealed covenant. He is named again among the Levites who set their seal (Neh 10:12), and a priest of the name blew with the trumpets before the ark in David's day (1Ch 15:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Shebaniah; in sacred history he is a Levite who led the confession and the blessing in the days of Nehemiah.
webster_full: SHEBANIAH, n. The LORD hath increased him; a proper name borne by Levites and priests.
A Levite who stood upon the stairs and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD.
He was among those who called the people to stand up and bless the LORD their God.
He set his seal to the covenant which the Levites made in the days of Nehemiah.
A priest of the name blew with the trumpets before the ark of God in the days of David.
scriptures: Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
Of Melicu, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;
corruption_summary: Corporate confession of the sins of the fathers is now dismissed as unjust inherited guilt, or else replaced with the ritual apologies of identity politics. Scripture teaches genuine covenant solidarity, and Nehemiah 9 shows what real confession looks like — addressed to God, resting on His character, and ending in obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand on either side of this chapter. The first says that no man can confess another's sin, that guilt is strictly individual, and that the Levites were indulging a primitive notion of inherited blame. The second, now common in the churches, borrows the form of Nehemiah 9 for the categories of modern grievance politics — corporate lament liturgies, generational apologies to demographic groups, penance offered horizontally to men rather than vertically to God, with no absolution possible because none is on offer. Both miss what the chapter does. Israel confesses to God, and the confession is answered by a covenant.

Scripture does hold real covenant solidarity: Daniel prays “We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments” (Dan 9:5), including himself in a guilt he had not personally incurred, and God commanded Israel to confess “their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers” (Lev 26:40). But Scripture equally holds personal accountability: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (Eze 18:20). The two are not in competition; the covenant community owns the sins of its history before God, and each man answers for his own. What makes Nehemiah 9 different from every modern imitation is its object and its end: it is spoken to a God whose glorious name is exalted above all blessing and praise, and it finishes not in perpetual lament but in a written covenant to obey.

pos: n. (a priest in the line of Aaron through Eleazar, ancestor of Zadok and of Ezra; and the head of a priestly house in the days of Joiakim)
etymology: From Hebrew Merayoth, from marah, to be rebellious or bitter — hence rebellious, or by another derivation from ra'ah, shewings. It is a hard name for a priest, and Scripture attaches no story to it that would explain the choice.
biblical_def: Meraioth is a link in the high-priestly descent, and he is named in three separate registers of it. The Chronicler gives the line from Aaron through Eleazar: “And Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth” (1Ch 6:6), and repeats it in the roll of those who ministered before the tabernacle: “Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son” (1Ch 6:52). Ezra traces his own descent through the same man when he introduces himself to the reader before going up from Babylon: “The son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth” (Ezr 7:3). And after the return, Seraiah the ruler of the house of God is reckoned “the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub” (Neh 11:11). A priestly house of the name is listed among the courses in the days of Joiakim: “Of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai” (Neh 12:15). Nothing is recorded of the man's life. What his name secures is the continuity of a priesthood by descent — the point on which the argument of Hebrews will eventually turn.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Meraioth; in sacred history he is a priest in the line of Eleazar the son of Aaron, and an ancestor of Ezra.
webster_full: MERAIOTH, n. A proper name in the priestly genealogies of Israel.
The son of Zerahiah, in the line of Eleazar the son of Aaron.
He was the father of Amariah and the ancestor of Ahitub and Zadok.
Ezra the scribe reckons his own descent through Meraioth.
A priestly house of the name is named among the courses in the days of Joiakim.
scriptures: And Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth,
Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son,
The son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth,
Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, was the ruler of the house of God.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the Aaronic priesthood was held by descent and therefore by dying men, and that Hebrews argues the superiority of Christ's priesthood from exactly that fact.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Meraioth is a name in a priestly register and nobody has contested him. What such lists exist to establish is that a man's right to serve at the altar rested on nothing but his descent — not his gifts, not his piety, not a call he felt. He could produce a genealogy or he could not, and after the captivity those who could not were put from the priesthood as polluted until a priest should stand up with Urim and with Thummim.

The principle to recover is the argument of Hebrews 7, which turns the genealogies into a doctrine of Christ. The Levitical priests “were many priests, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death” (Heb 7:23) — that is what a register like this one is, a list of funerals in the sanctuary — “But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood” (Heb 7:24). And Christ's title to serve came not by descent from Aaron at all, but after the order of Melchizedek, by the power of an endless life. Meraioth had a father and a son, and both are named, and both died. The Priest the church has now does not.
